claims.claim: Two archaeologists say Easter Island's platform statues were reshaped after they arrived.
claims.source_checked: Lipo & Hunt 2025, J. Archaeol. Sci. 183, 106383, doi:10.1016/j.jas.2025.106383: publisher's 18-page PDF as Firecrawl markdown (scratchpad lh25/lh25.md), read in full
claims.note: Two authors (Lipo, Binghamton anthropology; Hunt, Arizona School of Anthropology), writing archaeology in JAS. 1.1: platform shoulder/base ratios exceed 1.0; 'This modification occurred after transport, when carvers reduced the base width'; 'Platform moai, once they reached their destinations, were substantially modified through base reshaping'. 2.4: 'later modified to stand erect on ceremonial platforms'. 'Say' correctly attributes a reading whose only direct physical evidence in LH25 is a personal communication (S. Rapu 2011). Scope (platform statues) matches.

claims.claim: Dozens lie along the old roads from the quarry, apparently dropped on the way.
claims.note: 1.1: '62 statues documented along ancient transport roads, abandoned where they fell at various points of their journey from the Rano Raraku quarry'; roads 'radiate from Rano Raraku'. Fig. 12 says 84; 'dozens' fits both. 'Apparently' marks the transport-failure reading, which 2.5 records as disputed. Two (Fig. 7) are partly buried at an angle after re-erection attempts, not standing, so 'lie' holds.

claims.claim: On average, those statues have bases almost as wide as their shoulders, and they lean forward.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1016/j.jas.2025.106383, 1.1, 1.4, Figs. 1, 4, 5. NOT opened: doi:10.5281/zenodo.17329904 (Firecrawl credits exhausted; zenodo.org blocked by this sandbox's network)
claims.note: 1.1: road statues 'exhibit a shoulder-to-base width ratio approaching 1.0, meaning the base width nearly equals the shoulder width'; 'pronounced and consistent forward lean, typically ranging from 6 to 15 degrees'. 'On average' is narrower than the paper's text, so it passes A3 on LH25 alone. The corrected figures quoted in SOURCES entries 3 and 7 (1.025 +/- 0.155, n = 47) were not verified by this pass; do not put them on screen until someone opens the Zenodo record.

claims.claim: Rocked side to side with ropes, a statue like that steps forward.
claims.note: 1.1: 'Each lateral rocking motion thus produces a forward "step"'; Fig. 1: 'As moai is rocked side to side, it takes a step forward'; Fig. 9 same. Shown experimentally with a replica of road moai 12-220-01 that 'retained the same proportions and mass distribution' (1.4). Omitting the rear restraining rope does not make the line false.

claims.claim: In a test, eighteen people walked a scaled-down copy weighing over four tonnes a hundred meters in forty minutes.
claims.note: Abstract: 'precisely scaled 4.35 metric ton replica ... covering 100 m in 40 min with a team of 18 people'; 1.4: 'minimum crew of 18 individuals ... in one continuous effort, we achieved sustained forward movement of 100 m in just 40 min'; 1.6.3: '18 people were able to walk our replica moai a distance of 100 m in 40 min'. Scaled down: 1.4 original 'stands 7.35 m tall ... Our concrete replica, scaled for practical experimentation, weighed 4.35 metric tons'; 2.1 'a precise (scaled) copy'. 4.35 t = over four tonnes.

claims.claim: The statues on the platforms stand straight, and on average their bases are narrower than their shoulders.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1016/j.jas.2025.106383, 1.1, 2.4, Fig. 2. NOT opened: doi:10.5281/zenodo.17329904 (unreachable, see claim 3)
claims.note: 2.4: ahu moai 'stand vertically upright (bases flattened) with their center of mass positioned stably over their base'. 1.1: 'platform statues show ratios consistently exceeding 1.0, with shoulders wider than bases'; Fig. 2 reports the difference as significant. 'On average' is narrower than 'consistently', so the wording is supported by LH25 alone. SOURCES entry 7 says the published Fig. 2 is wrong per the authors' Zenodo note; this pass could not open that note, so the corrected numbers and the claim that the direction survives the correction are unverified here. Advisory, not a source failure: many platform statues were toppled and only some re-erected (not in LH25); a pedant may object to present-tense 'stand straight'. 'Were made to stand straight' would avoid that.

claims.claim: Eye sockets were carved only once a statue stood on its platform.
claims.note: 1.1: 'Ethnographic accounts and archaeological evidence confirm that eyes were carved only as a final step after the statue's successful erection on the platform'; 'only successful erection triggered the final transformation'. Matches as spoken. LH25 gives no citation for it, and those underlying accounts were not opened.

claims.claim: None of the road statues have them.
claims.note: 1.1: 'road moai uniformly lack carved eye sockets'; 'The complete absence of eye sockets on all 62 documented road moai'. The explicit count is for 62, and Fig. 12 counts 84, but 'uniformly' covers road moai in general. 'Road statues' is the neutral label, consistent with line 2's hedge.

claims.claim: So, they argue, the shape built for walking was carved away at the end of the journey.
claims.note: 2.4: 'ancestral engineers intentionally designed statues for walking'; 'Once the statues reached their destinations, these transport features were carved away to create stable, upright monuments'. 'They argue' attributes both the premise and the conclusion to the authors.

1: 'some scholars continue to reject the walking hypothesis'; critics named (Bahn, Flenley, Van Tilburg, Diamond, Velasco, Richards, Cauwe, De Dapper) are called 'established voices in Pacific archaeology'. Several are archaeologists (not Diamond or Flenley), so 'other archaeologists' holds. LH25 records no critic addressing the trimming claim itself; 'this' holds only because rejecting walking entails rejecting 'the shape built for walking'. Critics read only as LH25 reports them (disclosed in SOURCES, A2).

claims.claim: Some think many road statues were set up there on purpose.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1016/j.jas.2025.106383, 2.5, 2.5.2, 2.5.3, refs (Seager Thomas et al. 2023 title)
claims.note: 2.5: Richards et al. 2011, Seager Thomas et al. 2023, Cauwe & De Dapper 2015/2022 argue the statues 'were deliberately positioned along ceremonial paths ... rather than representing transport failures'; 2.5.2: Routledge/Heyerdahl 'positioned upright along a ceremonial pathway'; 2.5.3: Cauwe & De Dapper say 'isolated' moai were 'voluntary acts' that 'stood for perhaps centuries'. 'Set up' (upright), 'some' and 'many' (not all) fit. Their position as reported by their opponents, disclosed in SOURCES.

claims.claim: Hook (A4): what a viewer who swipes away at second two takes from line 1
claims.note: At about 2 s the viewer has heard 'Two archaeologists say Easter Island's...': the attribution comes first, so nothing is asserted as settled fact. The full sentence is attributed, limited to platform statues, and matches LH25 1.1 and 2.4. No false takeaway.
